name: Epic: Complete Spark collaborative settings, scenes, and evolution
description:
Execution: AFK after the first playable Spark slice.

User story:
As a group of writers, we can collaboratively define a thematic setting, frame scenes, challenge beliefs, and let both characters and the world evolve without losing authorship or decision history.

What to build:
Extend the Spark adapter with collaborative setting creation and campaign procedures: original inspiration notes, genre and facts, title, three setting Beliefs, GM attributes, Factions, Ties, Faces, Agendas, participant ownership, scene Platform, Tilt, and Question, collaboration and conflict phases, scene closing and reflection, belief replacement through Inspiration, character Growth, and setting Evolution. Represent setting entities in the adapter namespace with optional stable references into Weave World when that module is active.

Acceptance criteria:
- A group can create a setting through ordered, resumable contributions with explicit ownership, consent, revision history, and deterministic resolution of incomplete or concurrent edits.
- Setting Beliefs, Factions, Ties, Faces, and Agendas are typed, reference-safe, visible to story expressions, and portable without requiring a bundled setting.
- Scene framing records who supplied Platform, Tilt, and Question, validates the question and end condition, assigns the next responsibilities predictably, and feeds the existing Spark conflict loop.
- Inspiration and belief replacement require explicit participant confirmation, retain old and new belief lineage, grant Growth correctly, and trigger setting Evolution only when its conditions are satisfied.
- Evolution changes setting beliefs, attributes, and faction data through reviewable operations and never silently overwrites Weave World canon or canonical character personality data.
- Editor workflows support collaborative setup, scene framing, belief review, and evolution with equivalent source representations and accessible single-user fallbacks.
- Synthetic campaign fixtures use only original people, places, factions, inspirations, and themes and cover setup, several scenes, belief change, Growth, Evolution, save and restore, RON and JSON, Bevy, and PixiJS.
- Documentation separates the CC0 core procedures from Weave-authored collaboration UX and explains optional Weave World interoperation without importing published Spark settings.
result: Spark collaborative settings, scenes, and evolution are implemented: typed settings with factions, ties, faces, agendas, and optional world references; order-independent collaborative creation with retained revisions and resumable incomplete work; scene framing that opens the existing conflict loop; belief replacement with lineage and Growth; and setting Evolution with reviewed changes. description:

What to build:
Add deterministic character enrichment from year-only, month-day, or full birth dates. - A missing place, partial date, disputed source, or coarse observation produces bounded uncertainty or no candidate rather than fabricated precision.
- Coverage reports identify which requested dates and places have compatible data and why a context record was selected, skipped, or downgraded.

description:
Implement drag-to-reorder on the chapter card board and on the chapter tree. While a drag is in flight, draw an insertion bar in the gap between the two neighbouring cards the item would land between, using the accent colour. Acceptance criteria:
- Dragging a card shows an accent-coloured insertion bar in the gap at the target position
- Dropping a card reorders the siblings and persists the new order
- The moved item carries its whole subtree
- A container cannot be dropped into its own descendant
- The drop target is computed as a nearest-gap, so the pointer near a card edge still resolves to a single insertion point

- Undo restores the previous order

Insertion uses a nearest-gap computation over one card stride with wrapping rows, so a pointer near an edge resolves to exactly one gap. description:

Acceptance criteria:

- Every move and delete is undoable

name: Specify the tabletop ruleset adapter and license gate
description:
Execution: HITL architecture and licensing review.

User story:
As a module author, I can implement a tabletop ruleset through one stable public contract without adding adapter-specific branches throughout the parser, editor, runtime, or host integrations.

What to build:
Specify the adapter manifest, active-selection model, namespaced immutable definition and mutable state schemas, creation-step schema, capability vocabulary, deterministic resolver boundary, host-visibility rules, typed events, diagnostics, migrations, and authoring/runtime projections. Define how adapters may expose character creation, derived values, rolls or conflicts, resources, conditions, equipment, abilities, advancement, encounters, clocks, scenes, factions, and campaign state. Specify a conservative public-source gate for every bundled or third-party adapter.

Acceptance criteria:
- A project may install several adapters, select none or one primary adapter, and pin the resolved adapter ID, version, schema version, and content hash in compiled data.
- Canonical character data and adapter-owned data have distinct namespaces, authority, validation, and lifecycle rules; adapter suggestions never silently modify canonical values.
- Deterministic entropy consumption, save and restore, replay, hidden or host-only results, and structured resolver events are defined without depending on Bevy or PixiJS types.
- Capability discovery drives syntax validation and editor panels, and an absent capability fails with an actionable diagnostic rather than a partial fallback.
- Switching rules preserve canonical data, retain or archive inactive projections, preview incompatible state, and forbid automatic cross-system conversion unless an explicit reviewed migration exists.
- Canonical RON and JSON fixtures represent the same manifest, character projection, mutable state, and event payloads without semantic loss; invalid fixtures cover conflicts, unsupported versions, and undeclared capabilities.
- Provenance fields include source URL, exact artifact and revision, retrieval date, cryptographic hash, SPDX expression, covered files or sections, exclusions, attribution, required license text, and notices.
- The allowlist accepts verified CC0-1.0 inputs and separately licensed Apache-2.0 packs while rejecting unknown, ambiguous, non-allowlisted reciprocal or share-alike, noncommercial, no-derivatives, or otherwise unverified material.
- The design excludes unverified community supplements, logos, trade dress, and assets and uses system names only as factual compatibility labels without implying endorsement.
- The specification is independently written from first principles and includes a documented decision on declarative versus executable extension surfaces and crate boundaries.
result: Defined the separately versioned weave-tabletop adapter contract, deterministic resolver receipts and event visibility, neutral domain projection, editor capability catalog, license/provenance gate, JSON/RON schemas, synthetic fixtures, CLI validation, documentation, and end-to-end verification.

name: Switch active rulesets without corrupting character canon
description:
Execution: AFK after at least two structurally different adapters are complete.

User story:
As a writer, I can preview and change a character or campaign’s active ruleset while keeping canonical identity and personality intact and deciding deliberately what happens to system-specific state.

What to build:
Implement activation, deactivation, and switching among installed adapter projections. Resolve project or campaign defaults and permitted character overrides, preview field and capability changes, validate active play state, archive or discard inactive projections only through explicit policy, restore a prior projection when compatible, and distinguish same-adapter schema migration from cross-system conversion.

Acceptance criteria:
- A project can install several adapters while resolving exactly zero or one active primary adapter for a given character and play context, with deterministic inheritance and override rules.
- Switching never writes into canonical identity, HEXACO, derived OCEAN, alignment, birth or historical context, voice, inner-life, or author-canon fields.

- Inactive projections are namespaced and cannot affect expressions, events, editor panels, or host integrations until reactivated; archive, retain, and explicit discard policies are deterministic.
- Synthetic tests switch among Plug-And-Play, Dungeonpunk, and Freehack, including a switch during invalid active play state, archive and restoration, deactivation to no ruleset, save and reload, RON and JSON, Bevy, and PixiJS.
- Audit records explain who or what initiated the change, the old and new adapter identities and versions, decisions made, diagnostics, and preserved or discarded state without recording secrets.

name: Remove the redundant chapter body path field
description:
Outcome:
The chapter model has one join key for a body, not two.

Problem:
Chapter.body_path is documented as the path of the body relative to the manuscript directory, but nothing sets it and nothing reads it. ChapterTree::add_chapter always writes None, and BodyStore derives its path from the chapter id. The field is therefore always None, and a reader who trusts it would conclude that no chapter has a body.

It also contradicts the recorded design: the tree and the bodies are joined by id, which is what makes a reorder a single-field write and lets a body file be found without consulting the tree.

Requirements:
- Remove the field from the model rather than populating a second source of truth.
- Keep the id as the only join key between a tree record and a body file.
- Regenerate the example corpus without the field.
- Keep the documented architecture and the editor guide accurate.

Acceptance criteria:
- The chapter record no longer carries a body path.
- BodyStore is the only place a body location is derived.
- The corpus still loads and its tests still pass.
- No documentation claims a stored body path.
result: Removed Chapter.body_path. The field was always None because add_chapter never set it and BodyStore derives a body location from the chapter id, so it was dead weight that misrepresented the model. The chapter id is now the single join key between the tree and a body file, matching the documented design. Regenerated the example corpus without the field and updated the editor guide.

commit.message: refactor(editor): drop the unused chapter body path

name: Render the chapter tree and card board
description:
Render the manuscript's ordered children as the two structural surfaces the model was built for: a tree that shows the hierarchy, and a card board that shows the selected container's children as cards.

Both surfaces read one shared projection of the ordered child list, the same projection the table will read next, so a selection, a filter, or a reorder cannot disagree between them. The tree is the navigation surface: it shows the whole hierarchy, marks the current chapter, and is what drag-to-reorder and the status bar attach to. Splitting the tree into a separate task was a planning gap; it belongs here because it is the first consumer of the projection.

The card is a text surface, not a picture of a document. Its accessible name should convey the item and its position, for example Chapter (1 of 2 index cards).

Acceptance criteria:
- The tree renders the whole hierarchy in stored order, marks the selection, and exposes each row's title and kind
- Selecting a container renders its children as cards in the same order the tree shows
- A card header shows the icon, the title, and a separator rule
- A card body shows the chapter's text, truncated to a readable amount
- The card's accessible name states the title and its ordinal among the cards
- A container with no children shows an explicit empty state naming the container
- Cards reflow to a configurable number of columns with a fixed aspect ratio
- Both surfaces read the same projection, and neither keeps its own copy of the order
- A tree row is addressable for the later drag, move, and status work without reworking the projection
result: Added a Manuscript center view with a chapter tree and a card board over one shared projection. The projection is plain data and unit tested: tree order and depth, selection resolving to the parent container for leaves, card ordinals, accessible names, empty states, column clamping, and word-boundary excerpt truncation. The tree renders the whole hierarchy with per-row kind colour and selection, and the board renders fixed 260x176 cards with a header icon, title, separator rule, clamped body excerpt, and word count, reflowing to a configurable column count. name: Determine cross-container drag and drop behaviour
description:
Unknown from the research: what happens when a card is dropped onto a card in a different container, whether a container can be dropped into its own descendant in practice, whether autoscroll happens near the edge of the card area, and whether the insertion indicator differs for a drop before versus after a card.

Only a reorder within one container was exercised. Cross-container moves are the other half of the feature, and they are what a user will try first when reorganising a manuscript across parts.

How to close it: drive a drag from the card board of one container to the card board of another, and to a node in the tree, capturing a screenshot of the indicator at each target. Record the answer in research/scrivener/notes/04-drag-and-drop.md.

- The behaviour of a tree-to-tree drop is established
- Whether dropping onto a card nests the item is established

result: A card dragged from one container's board onto a tree row in another container is reparented, confirmed by the persisted project file: the scene's BinderItem changed parent and the source container lost a child. The affordance for a container drop is not an insertion bar: the target tree row is highlighted in the accent colour and a live preview of the dragged card, including its title and body, is drawn as a floating overlay. A reorder within a container instead draws a vertical accent-coloured insertion bar in the gap between the two cards and outlines the source card. The insertion point is a nearest-gap computation: hovering the top and the bottom of a card produce the same bar, and dragging past the last card removes the bar entirely. The 'before' and 'after' positions are not distinguished on this build. name: Add a provenance-tracked public-domain example corpus
description:
Status: this task delivers the corpus data and its verification. Rendering the corpus in the editor surfaces is o97au6iq's job.

Execution: AFK. Pairs with o97au6iq: the surfaces need real prose to be judged, not three synthetic chapters.

Outcome:
Weave ships a small, provenance-tracked corpus of public-domain manuscripts that an author can open as a real project and that tests can use as realistic fixtures.

Synthetic fixtures stay for precise assertions. This corpus exists because a card board, a table, a word count, and a manuscript format are only meaningful against real chapter structure.

Candidate works, all first published before 1931 and in the United States public domain:
- Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Lewis Carroll, 1865. Twelve chapters, one level deep. Standard Ebooks edition, illustrated by John Tenniel, 26,738 words.
- The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes, Arthur Conan Doyle, 1892. Twelve stories, each with numbered sections, so the tree is three levels deep and reparenting is exercised.
- The Time Machine, H. G. Wells, 1895. Sixteen short chapters; the smallest complete novel of the set.
- The Importance of Being Earnest, Oscar Wilde, 1895. Three acts of dialogue; the natural source for a Play scene fixture.
- Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones, 1912. Many very short items, useful for large sibling lists.

Source rules:
- Prefer Standard Ebooks. Its editions are US public domain and it dedicates its editorial work under CC0, with one Git repository per book, so the exact revision is pinnable.
- Project Gutenberg text is public domain, but its licence and trademark cover the ebook wrapper. If it is used, strip every Project Gutenberg reference and do not use the name.
- A translation carries its own copyright. Only use translations published before 1931 and record the translator.
- Exclude illustrations and cover art unless separately cleared and recorded. This corpus is text.

Requirements:
- Commit a curated subset per work rather than a whole library, with a documented size budget.
- Record per work: title, author, first publication year, translator when relevant, source URL, upstream revision, retrieval date, licence expression, and every transformation applied.
- Convert each work into a Weave manuscript project: ordered chapters, a body per chapter, and the project-level style sheet.
- Keep the conversion deterministic and re-runnable.

Acceptance criteria:
- A provenance file lists every work with source, revision, licence, and transformation notes.
- The corpus loads through the manuscript store, and tests assert tree validity and body isolation for every work. Rendering it in the tree and card board belongs to o97au6iq.
- Word counts for the committed subset match the recorded source counts.
- No fixture contains a Project Gutenberg reference or uncleared artwork.
- A regeneration check fails when a committed body no longer matches its recorded source hash.
result: Added four Standard Ebooks public-domain manuscripts as editor projects: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland (12 titled chapters), The Time Machine (12 chapters and an epilogue), The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (one story split into three numbered scenes and one flat story), and 20 Aesop fables as leaf scenes. Each work carries provenance.json with source URL, CC0 licence, retrieval date, edition hash, and per-chapter source, paragraph and word counts, text hash, and body hash. No Project Gutenberg material and no artwork. scripts/build-corpus.py fetches, converts, and verifies offline; verification is wired into scripts/build-docs.py. editor/tests/corpus.rs loads every project through ManuscriptStore and asserts tree validity, trash ordering, nested scenes, body isolation, and word-count parity.

- Move Up/Down/Left/Right work from a menu and a shortcut, backed by one shared handler
- The chapter body is stored separately from the tree structure
- Deleting a chapter moves it to a visible Trash container

See research/scrivener/notes/07-ux-flow.md for the full rationale and the source observations.
result: Delivered the chapter authoring experience. The manuscript model stores one ordered child list per container with an explicit order and a body file per chapter. One shared projection renders as a tree, a card board, and a metadata table with a shared filter and windowed rows. Status and label are ID-backed, editable from the tree row, the table, and the window status bar, with a Settings surface that adds and renames definitions without rewriting records. Move up, down, promote, and demote plus move-to-front, trash, restore, and empty-trash share one handler across the toolbar, the Chapter menu, and the keyboard, and every structural change is undoable. Drag reordering draws an insertion bar in the gap and reparents onto tree rows. A Write view renders the manuscript page with margins, line guides, typographic styles, live word count, and per-chapter caret persistence. Four public-domain books provide real material, and 175 tests cover the model, projection, editing, layout, and session.

name: Add the chapter table with inline metadata editing
description:
Render the same ordered child list as a table of rows, alongside the tree and the card board. This is the dense editing surface: each row shows the document and lets metadata be edited in place.

The table is a projection of the same list the card board renders, not a separate data source, so a filter applied to one applies to the other. Give the table configurable visible columns, with the first column carrying the document title and further columns carrying status, label, and section type as inline editors.

- The table renders the same children, in the same order, as the card board
- A row edits status, label, and section type in place without leaving the table
- Visible columns are configurable and the selection persists

- The row count reflects the filtered set

result: Added a Table mode beside the card board over the same projection, so the filtered set and order cannot diverge. name: Epic: Selectable tabletop rulesets for Weave Character
description:
Outcome:
Ship optional, versioned tabletop-ruleset adapters that let an author choose no ruleset or one primary ruleset for a character or campaign, create the system-specific character data, and use the same rules state through Weave source, the editor, the standalone runtime, RON, JSON, Bevy, and PixiJS.

Requirements:
- Keep the canonical Weave Character Profile system-neutral. Store every tabletop projection and mutable rules state under a stable, versioned adapter namespace.
- Allow multiple compatible adapters to be installed while resolving at most one active primary adapter per character or campaign. Support adapter-owned optional modules without mixing unrelated resolution systems.
- Declare capabilities for character creation, derived statistics, checks and conflicts, resources and conditions, equipment and abilities, advancement, encounters, clocks, scenes, factions, and world or campaign state.
- Use deterministic seeded resolution and serializable state so replay, save, reload, editor preview, and host integrations agree.
- Never infer physical, intellectual, social, or supernatural statistics silently from personality, alignment, birth data, or historical context. Suggestions must be explainable and require author acceptance.
- Initially support verified official artifacts for Open Adventure, Dungeonpunk, Freehack, Plug-And-Play, Spark, Wicked Ones, and Open Tale.

Acceptance criteria:
- A writer can choose a supported adapter in text or the editor, complete its character-creation flow, validate the result, compile it, and access namespaced rules data at runtime.
- System-specific checks, resources, conditions, advancement, and optional campaign features are exposed only when the selected adapter declares them.
- The canonical Character Profile survives adapter activation, deactivation, and switching without silent mutation or lossy conversion.
- Equivalent versioned RON and JSON outputs are consumed by focused Bevy and PixiJS examples.
- Every bundled adapter records the exact upstream artifact, version or date, content hash, source URL, SPDX license, covered material, exclusions, and required notices.
- Only verified CC0 material and the separately identified Apache-2.0 Open Tale pack are included. Factual compatibility names do not imply endorsement, and unverified logos, trade dress, community supplements, or assets are absent.
result: Selectable tabletop rulesets are complete: seven adapters with manifests, resolvers, conformance registration, source policies, fixtures, and a catalog; ruleset switching with archives, audits, and migration; and a conformance suite that verifies every adapter's contract and bundle. Verified by the full tabletop suite, clippy, and rustfmt.

name: Expose presentation cues to browser player callers
description:
Outcome:
A JavaScript caller using the browser player can read the presentation cues produced by an advance, not only the line, choices, and pattern draws.

Problem:
The wasm binding throws a plain JS error on failure and exposes no cue accessor, so a browser renderer cannot drive the same scene contract the editor and Bevy consume. The native PlayerFrame already carries cues; only the JS boundary is missing.

Requirements:
- Expose presentation cues for each successful advance and for a failed advance, matching the native PlayerFrame and PlayerFailure shapes.
- Keep the cue order identical to the native API.
- Do not change the save-state format.

Acceptance criteria:
- A wasm test advances a cue-bearing story and observes the ordered cues.
- A failed advance exposes the cues that ran before the failure.
- The binding adds no second runtime and no editor dependency.
result: The wasm boundary and example player now surface presentation cues. A successful advance returns the ordered cues; a failed advance returns PlayerFailure carrying the cues produced before the failure, matching the editor and Bevy rule. The example player applies scene cues as a background, resolves a speaker to the declared stage name, and falls back when a field is absent. The fixture gains a scene, stage, speaker cue, and synthetic SVG background. Save-state format unchanged; six web player tests pass.

commit.message: feat(web): surface presentation cues to browser callers
